article_text:
Films and events

Galas

Ink

The Mayor of London’s Gala

Danny Boyle brings a seismic moment in Rupert Murdoch’s Fleet Street career blazingly to life, employing the breathtaking style of a story torn from the headlines.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Screening at cinemas around the UK – find out more .

Credits

Director Danny Boyle

Screenwriter James Graham

With Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce, Claire Foy

UK 2026. 118min

Courtesy of STUDIOCANAL

Language English

Access information

Monday 12 October 21:00

Audio description

Closed Captions (CC) via WatchWord smart glasses

Tuesday 13 October 11:00

Audio description

Descriptive subtitles

Sunday 18 October 10:20

Audio description

Descriptive subtitles

Find out about booking access tickets

Introduction

In 1969, Rupert Murdoch acquired British tabloid The Sun, hiring gifted editor Larry Lamb to change the paper’s fortunes. Out of this devil’s pact, British journalism and society was forever changed. Boyle’s kinetic cinematic energy is matched by Guy Pearce and Jack O’Connell’s muscular performances as the men who exploded Fleet Street, British mores and political fortunes.

Kristy Matheson

Content advice

Contains scenes of drug use, graphic violence or injury, nudity, and sex.

Contains sexist attitudes and language.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Screen Talk: Danny Boyle

The director of Ink joins us for this Screen Talk, to discuss a career that has placed him among the most successful British filmmakers.

All About the Money

The heir of one of America’s wealthiest families, who has ambitions to rebel against values he now despises, is the subject of Sinéad O’Shea’s compelling documentary portrait.

Tender Loving Care

In a world that feels increasingly untethered from human connection, the incomparable Mike Leigh returns with a thought-provoking and compassionate view of urban life.

article_text:
Source: Anders Overgaard

Jesper Just, Trine Dyrholm, Christian Slater, Dree Hemingway

Trine Dyrholm, Christian Slater and Dree Hemingway have signed to star in Jesper Just’s Incidents Of Intimacy , the second feature film from Denmark’s Dogma 25 filmmaking initiative.

The film will follow a woman who steals objects from people to file them in an archive until they begin to take on a life of their own. The film is scheduled for a theatrical release in 2027.

Danish actors Johannes Lilleore, Julie Agnete Vang, Laura Drasbaek and Michael Moritzen will also star.

The film is written by Danish artist-filmmaker Just in collaboration with Sissel Dalsgaard Thomsen, who previously wrote Isabella Eklof’s Kalak and Malene Choi’s The Quiet Migration .

Incidents Of Intimacy is his first feature. His work as an artist has been shown at exhibitions including the Venice Biennale.

Dogma 25

It is the second Danish Dogma 25 title to head towards production after Eklof’s Mr. Nawashi . All five films are being produced by Zentropa. The projects are financed in a collaboration between Zentropa, DR, and Nordisk Film Distribution, with the addition of Netflix, which has taken Nordic streaming rights.

Incidents Of Intimacy has also received support from the Danish Film Institute, the Eastern Denmark Film Fund and Nordisk Film & TV Fond.

Nordisk Film Distribution will release the Dogma 25 films theatrically in the region. TrustNordisk handles international sales on the titles.

The rebirth of the Dogma filmmaking movement in the Nordics last year has been followed by similar initiatives in Germany and the UK , both launched in Cannes this year.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : Indie rom-com movie Crazy Rich Arabs (no relation to WB’s Crazy Rich Asians franchise) kicks off in LA next week with cast led by Omar Sharif Jr . ( The Secret Scripture ), Sam Asghari ( Hacks ), Aron Kader ( Ramy ), and Walid Chaya ( The Blacklist: Redemption ).

The ensemble also features Kourosh Parsapour ( In the Garden of Tulips ), Lara J Barry ( Where Murder Lies ), Sarah Siadat ( Veep ), George Khouri ( Funny or Die ), and newcomers Sophia Konat and Maya Tannous.

Directed by Peter Takla and co-written by Chaya and Jimmy Monack, with Chaya and Sharif Jr. serving as executive producers, the story “follows Youssef (Walid Chaya), a sheltered musician from Beirut who travels to Los Angeles for an arranged marriage with Reema (Sophia Konat), whose protective brother (George Khouri) isn’t easily impressed. His plans take an unexpected turn when he discovers Omar (also played by Chaya), his long-lost identical twin and a wealthy Hollywood divorce attorney. When the brothers switch identities, romance, family secrets, and cultural clashes spiral into chaos, drawing in Omar’s best friend Layla (Maya Tannous), a Beverly Hills lounge owner, and charming Airbnb host Shay (Omar Sharif Jr.).”

Related Stories

Evan Mirzai Preps Adaptation Of Sheeva Moshiri's Rom-Com 'The Cupid Index' With Shiva Negar, Alexander Uloom & Sam Asghari

'Grand Death Lotto': Paul Feig's Amazon Action Comedy Adds Eight

Original music and soundtrack will come from Rawan Chaya. Chaya’s Moonlit Wings Productions produces.

Watch on Deadline

According to Chaya, the production aims to challenge “Hollywood’s longstanding underrepresentation of Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) characters, particularly in leading roles”: “By placing Arab-American characters at the center of a glamorous, heartfelt comedy, the film offers a perspective rarely seen in mainstream romantic storytelling.”

He continued: “Growing up, I rarely saw people who looked like me represented on screen, especially in stories that celebrated our culture rather than reinforced stereotypes. With Crazy Rich Arabs , we’re changing that—bringing Arab characters to the forefront through humor, heart, and a universal story about love, family, and what it really means to live a rich life.”

article_text:
Pegah Ahangurani’s “ Rehearsals for a Revolution ” is one of the year’s most powerful films, combining half a century of Iranian history with the director’s own personal story of being exiled to London. It all forms one powerful tapestry that begins with a single word: “Yad.”

The Persian word for memory and remembrance ties the entire film together, allowing Ahangurani and editor Arash Ashtiani to weave timelines together under the idea that memory is its own form of revolution. At our Art of the Doc event in Los Angeles, the duo sat down with IndieWire editor-in-chief Brent Lang for a wide-ranging conversation that began with the film’s opening word.

“I wanted to emphasize the act of remembering, because the central idea of my film is about remembering,” Ahangurani said. “I grew up in Iran and I’ve lived there my whole life, and I know very well that the authoritarians, including the one in Iran, they don’t only censor people. They also try to erase our memories, erase our past, and replace it with their own version of history. They try to rewrite it, and we shouldn’t let them steal our memories. I think remembering is one of the few things we have. We should remember our past, we should remember our victims, we should mourn them. Only after that can we start to heal.”

Watch the complete conversation in the video above.

National Geographic Documentary Films, part of a joint venture between The Walt Disney Company and the National Geographic Society, is committed to bringing the world premium, feature documentaries that cover timely, provocative and globally relevant stories from the very best documentary filmmakers. Its award-winning and critically acclaimed films reach 300 million people worldwide in 180 countries and 33 languages across the global National Geographic channels and direct-to-consumer platforms Disney+ and Hulu.

Recent films include the Emmy-nominated winner of the IDA Award for Best Feature “The Tale of Silyan;” Oscar® and Peabody nominee “Sugarcane;” Oscar-nominated and Peabody Award winner “Bobi Wine: The People’s President;” Emmy Award winner “Lost In The Jungle;” Oscar- and BAFTA-nominated “Fire of Love;” Emmy and Peabody Award winner “The Territory;” BAFTA nominees “The Rescue” and “Becoming Cousteau;” and Oscar- and BAFTA winner “Free Solo.” For more information visit films.nationalgeographic.com , or find us on Facebook , Twitter , Instagram , and YouTube .

article_text:
Feature

Why Pageant Is Suddenly All the Rage

In a world skewed toward artifice, the East Williamsburg performance space’s commitment to confronting, rather than escaping, one’s conditions in art feels like a renaissance.

On a Friday morning in late August, dozens packed a small auditorium at the Museum of Modern Art to watch choreographer, director, and writer Isa Spector writhe on a red-painted platform, struggling to carry out the museum’s request to make “a painting of dance” in 10 minutes. After flailing to and fro, down on all fours to the red platform floor and up to the fluorescent studio lights, and calling out to a "mom" whose name changed to “MoMA” and a "dad" to “Dada” with an alliterative tongue, Spector had an epiphany. They knew what they were to paint. Seconds later, five performers donning red gloves emerged from backstage and assembled at the center of the platform. Hand in hand, they began twirling in a circle, staging a living parody of Matisse’s modernist masterpiece displayed in the galleries just a floor above.

The five subjects of this commissioned “painting” — Sharleen Chidiac, Lili Dekker, Jade Manns, Owen Prum, and Alexa West — are the co-founders of Pageant , an artist-run Brooklyn performance space that held a month-long residency at MoMA in August. "MoMAlogue #1" inaugurated Pageant’s seven-hour MoMA performance marathon, of which Spector’s was the first, but certainly not the only, meditation on dance’s relationship to its own history and that of visual art across 25 10-minute performances.

“I think the history of dance, coming from a ballet proscenium stage into modernism, then into postmodernism, started with a pictorial form,” artist and choreographer West said in a group interview with Hyperallergic after the Pageant Presents Pageant marathon. “And it’s slowly been breaking away from that over time.”

Preceded by a different space that Manns and Chidiac ran out of their apartment, Pageant was established in 2022 in a third-story loft on Graham Avenue in East Williamsburg. According to West, there was initially “no clear marketing vision” for Pageant. It was merely a solution to the group’s shared desire “to provide context to our practices in a post-COVID landscape in which there were very few opportunities to show work at our stage of artmaking.”

“We didn’t set out with the intention for it to be like an institution,” Chidiac added during the interview. “We just needed a space to work, to show our work, and to show other people’s work.

title_original: Valérie Naessens
editorial_title_zh: Valérie Naessens
editorial_excerpt_zh: 渐浓的夜色 当你揉去睡意，脑海中会留存下什么影像？在《The Gathering Dark》中，瓦莱丽·纳森斯（Valérie Naessens）涉足了灵魂低语与潜意识依恋的领域 […] 这篇关于瓦莱丽·纳森斯的文章最初出现在《摄影之眼》杂志上。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "渐浓的夜色", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当你揉去睡意，脑海中会留存下什么影像？在《The Gathering Dark》中，瓦莱丽·纳森斯涉足了灵魂低语与潜意识依恋的领域。每一张影像都是通往梦想者内心世界的一扇窗。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这个系列超越了逻辑的边界。正如梦境中的大脑将零散的记忆与印象交织在一起，纳森斯也将那些初看似乎无关的碎片融合。她在潜意识中梦游，抛下了种种规则与限制。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "阴影错位。细节模糊，仿佛遗忘已经开始。其他元素则通过色彩对比脱颖而出。一切都很重要，却又一切都无足轻重。没有清晰的开始或结尾。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "什么是真实，什么是幻觉？你在对自己讲述怎样的故事？信念与体验之间的界限有多薄？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在与朋友度假期间，瓦莱丽·纳森斯在夜里被自己的尖叫声惊醒。她的精神掌控了身体，打破了睡眠。朋友们也醒了。他们在早餐时的追问，以及她与梦境之间微妙不安的关系，构成了这个系列的基础。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她渴望忘掉自己在睡梦中所见的一切。然而，夜晚依然令她着迷。当房屋入睡，一切各得其所，为存在与观察创造了空间。夜晚是世界的暂停键；所有锋利的边缘都消失了，只留下本质。黑暗铺开了一层宁静的毯子，让人得以轻柔着地。你转向内收，随后它们便自然浮现：那些随机的记忆与印象，犹如置身梦中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Https://www.valerienaessens.be/en/home/", "links": [{"text": "Https://www.valerienaessens.be/en/home/", "url": "https://www.valerienaessens.be/en/home/"}], "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "The gathering dark"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "What images linger when you rub the sleep from your eyes? In “The Gathering Dark,” Valérie Naessens ventures to the realm where the soul speaks and the subconscious clings. Each image is a window into the dreamer’s inner world."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This series transcends the boundaries of logic. Just as the brain in dreams weaves together random memories and impressions, Naessens melds fragments that initially seem unrelated. She sleepwalks through the subconscious, shedding rules and restrictions."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Shadows misalign. Details blur, as if forgetting has already begun. Other elements stand out through color contrast. Everything is important, yet nothing is. There is no clear beginning or end."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "What is real and what is illusion? What story are you telling yourself? How thin is the line between belief and experience?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "During a holiday with friends, Valérie Naessens is jolted awake at night by her own screams. Her mind seizes control of her body, ending her sleep. Friends awaken too. article_text:
The gathering dark

What images linger when you rub the sleep from your eyes? In “The Gathering Dark,” Valérie Naessens ventures to the realm where the soul speaks and the subconscious clings. Each image is a window into the dreamer’s inner world.

This series transcends the boundaries of logic. Just as the brain in dreams weaves together random memories and impressions, Naessens melds fragments that initially seem unrelated. She sleepwalks through the subconscious, shedding rules and restrictions.

Shadows misalign. Details blur, as if forgetting has already begun. Other elements stand out through color contrast. Everything is important, yet nothing is. There is no clear beginning or end.

What is real and what is illusion? What story are you telling yourself? How thin is the line between belief and experience?

During a holiday with friends, Valérie Naessens is jolted awake at night by her own screams. Her mind seizes control of her body, ending her sleep. Friends awaken too. Their questions at breakfast and her uneasy relationship with dreams form the basis for the series.

She longs to forget what she saw in her sleep. Yet, the night continues to enchant her. When the house sleeps, everything falls into place, creating space to be and observe. The night is the world’s pause button; all sharp edges disappear, leaving only the essence. Darkness spreads a blanket of tranquility, allowing a soft landing. You turn inward, and then they loom naturally: the random memories and impressions, as in a dream.

article_text:
Director Ueda Shinichiro made a name for himself with filmmaking that has embraced self-reflexivity: the beloved cult zombie film “ One Cut of the Dead ” was continually transforming, from a single-take horror-comedy into a meditation on the act of filmmaking and then the chaos of actually being on set.

His new feature “ Earthlings in Love ,” showing in the Nippon Cinema Now section of the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival , brings that interest in how filmmaking influences us into a curious new space: the vertically shot, social media-friendly microdrama.

Related Stories

Disney Names Carol Choi Asia Pacific President as Luke Kang Retires

“Earthlings in Love” follows Shinpei, a director who discovers that he has young-onset dementia. Setting out on a journey to record his memories, he decides to finish shooting a film he began making with friends as a teenager. The film began as a series of 30 short episodes released on social media, each only a few minutes long. According to Ueda, an enthusiastic online response encouraged its adaptation to feature length and a theatrical release. Variety spoke to Ueda about bridging the gap between mediums, and about filmmaking about filmmaking.

Was the method of vertical filming decided before the script was written, or after?

Vertical first, and then we thought of the screenplay. The work itself was not originally conceived as a feature film – I did plan it as an idea for vertical social media, but I think I have more of a nature that fits feature films, and that’s what I’ve been doing.

[As for] where the storytelling and the concept come from, I visited my local town and met my old schoolmates there. We were having drinks, and when we were talking about memories, I realized that there were some differences in how we interpreted the same events we had experienced, and some things that were completely forgotten. So my own experience is the basis for some part of the story. I wanted to create a story about the difference between memory and what has been recorded.

What appealed to you about filming this way, and what took readjustment in how you frame scenes with less horizontal space?

I believe that the aspect ratio really fits human [proportions] very well. [While] it’s a good format for shooting one person, when it comes to group shots, there are some challenges and restrictions.

The vertical frame often, deliberately, leaves out information that we then discover later from a different angle. Was that intentional?

That is how I took some advantage of it – it leaves things to the viewer’s imagination. There’s also another thing, because the topic here is young-onset dementia. You may know that some symptoms of dementia do limit vision. So the vertical format, with its omitted areas of vision, actually does have a connection with that as well.

You’re also the editor on your films – what changed in the rhythm of your editing between this story as an internet series and as a feature?

The total [runtime] of all 30 episodes was 76 minutes when we originally released it on social media. When we re-edited it for the feature film, it became 111 minutes. On social media, you always have to be mindful about keeping people’s attention. If you make it too slow, they’re just going to swipe away to different content. But with the feature version, once they come to the theater and they’re seated, you know that they’re not going to go away. You can get their attention for two hours. So I could take advantage of that and spend time on the direction, making sure that I show off the acting, on the assumption that they’re going to focus for a while.

With the runtime increasing, were you reintroducing footage you had already shot, or were there reshoots?

Both – there were some shots and some lines that I couldn’t include in the social media version, which I added back into the feature. We did some additional shooting too. Also, there were some things in the social media version, cliffhanger scenes to entice people to watch the next day, that I didn’t need in the feature, so I cut some of them out.

How did it compare to shooting “One Cut of the Dead” or “Special Actors”?

The obvious difference is the vertical frame, but to be very honest, apart from that, I didn’t change my approach from feature films. When you think about actors in Japan, or maybe globally as well, in short dramas or a vertical format they tend to overact. The output is a bit bigger. But the actors in my work have acting experience in feature films anyway, so their performances were of the quality they would give in feature films. So besides the format, there wasn’t a big difference.

You’d released a number of microdramas before – what did you learn from them that you brought forward into “Earthlings in Love”?

When I think [about] what I learned or what the main difference is, it’s not about how I shoot or make the work itself. It’s more the reactions of the viewers: it’s so fast. As soon as you release something, you see the comments filling up the space on the social media platform.

To give you a very extreme example, I might come up with an idea in the morning, shoot it in the daytime and release it in the evening. It’s like making a comment or tweeting something. With a feature film, you have to start planning, and it’s going to take 12 months at least until it gets into the theater.

Because you’ve worked both in the theatrical format and in the microdrama space, do you feel that the theatrical space will continue to be valued?

I think both will exist over time. I even think that the vertical shorts market will grow further, but the theaters will stay. Because, at least in Japan, it is now the only place where people will turn off their phones and sit together for two hours, listening to or watching something. I’m borrowing this phrase from a senior director friend of mine, but he said that it’s like a church or a sacred place, because you sit in the darkness, you’re all together, and you’re listening to [someone] preaching, right? It is like a ritual, one that will stay, because it’s very unique and it’s the only place where it works this way.

article_text:
The director Jonathan Glazer said he was “shocked into silence” the first time he watched NAZA, an award-winning documentary about Israel’s systems of mass killing in the war on Gaza.

Glazer appeared on a panel at NAZA’s UK premiere in London on Thursday night alongside key figures behind the documentary, including its Israeli co-directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.

Since the film’s release, the Israeli government has denounced it and pursued those involved, announcing plans aimed at stripping citizenship from Abraham and Szor, who government ministers have accused of treason.

Responding to questions from the Guardian’s editor-in-chief, Katharine Viner, who chaired the event, Glazer, who is an executive producer on the film, said he was “shocked into silence” the first time he watched NAZA , which is produced by the Guardian.

“It wasn’t really a question for me of getting involved once Yuval and Rachel had asked me to,” he said. “Partly because of the power of the testimonies. But also the filmmaking: the way they had presented those testimonies was cinematic and eloquent in terms of form.”

He noted that NAZA was “clearly in dialogue” with and “deals with very similar themes” to The Zone of Interest, the 2023 historical drama he directed and that depicted the mundane daily lives of Nazi officers overseeing the extermination of Jews at Auschwitz.

“Both films deal with dehumanisation,” Glazer said. “And how we get to where we do as a species by othering and dehumanising, and what that then leads to.”

Asked whether he was surprised by the intense reaction of the Israeli government to NAZA, Glazer replied: “We had conversations before the film about what Yuval and Rachel were anticipating. But certainly from my point of view [the reaction] was much more venal than I thought it was going to be.”

Glazer’s long-time collaborator, James Wilson, who was a producer on NAZA, made similar remarks at the BFI London Film Festival earlier this month. Wilson condemned the “hysterical, vituperative, aggressive backlash from members of the Israeli government and Israeli politicians.”

Expanding on those comments on Thursday, Wilson noted how the Israeli government reaction occurred before anyone in the country had even seen the film. He said while the response in Israel makes him “angry” he believes it reveals something about “perpetrator psyche”. “When confronted by reality, it’s the rage of cognitive dissonance.”

Abraham said the film allows viewers to look at the “mechanisms that allow human beings to do this to other human beings”, and Szor said the idea to shoot footage looking inside Tel Aviv citizens’ apartments was to focus on the “ritual” of people gathering around the TV to watch the “news and to see the absence or justification” of the devastation happening in Gaza .

She said she and Abraham began recording interviews before they had begun thinking about the form or visual language of the film. “We thought this is our responsibility as Israelis who have access to [soldiers and officers involved in the war in Gaza] to try to just record those interviews.”

Paul Lewis, the Guardian’s head of investigations, and an executive producer on NAZA, said many other Israeli journalists would not have done this work because of the risks. He said of Abraham and Szor: “They deserve a huge plaudit from everyone for their courage. There is a cost to them both. The response from the Israeli government is absolutely appalling. No-one who works as a filmmaker or a journalist should be punished for an exercise in telling the truth.”

NAZA is in UK cinemas and will be shown in more than 50 countries. As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November. When the film opened in Italy last month, it surpassed the Marvel movie Avengers Endgame: Encore to open at No 1.

The film contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders who detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge that large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.

Various bodies, including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based, have said Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

The film premiered at the Venice film festival, where it was met with a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went on to win the special jury prize .

Israeli government officials have attempted to discredit NAZA’s content, while far-right activists have threatened to hunt down the directors.

The Israel Defense Forces’ chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, has said they will use “every tool at our disposal” against the film, while the military has issued a 10-page response to NAZA, which was based on interviews with more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.

Demonstrators have gathered outside the home of Szor’s parents, demanding that she face the death penalty, and a mural depicting the film-makers through the sights of a gun appeared in the Israeli city of Ashdod.

Szor and Abraham addressed the backlash to their documentary at a Q&A after its New York premiere. “Our country is doing so much to hide these systems,” Szor told the audience. “It’s not a world that is open even to the Israeli public.”

The Zone of Interest won the Oscar for best international film in 2024.

article_text:
Elke Sommer, the prolific German star of the Pink Panther film A Shot in the Dark, early 70s Agatha Christie adaptation And Then there Were None, and British sex comedy Carry on Behind, has died aged 85. Bild magazine reported that Sommer died in Los Angeles of heart failure.

German-born Sommer, whose best-known film roles were in the 1960s and 70s, was one of the wave of European performers who crossed over to Hollywood and English-language cinema with considerable success, following the postwar emergence of European new wave cinema. Sommer was one of the few German actors to make waves at the time, as Hollywood made much of her bombshell image.

Born Elke Schletz in 1940 in Berlin, the daughter of a Protestant pastor, she was evacuated with her family to Bavaria during the war. Intending to work as an interpreter, she was spotted by celebrated Italian director Vittorio De Sica after winning a beauty contest on a trip to Italy in 1958, and subsequently offered roles in a string of Italian comedy films. She crossed back into more serious work with the West German drama The Death Ship, opposite Horst Buchholz (who would go on to appear in cowboy classic The Magnificent Seven).

With her gift for languages, Sommer made her first film in English, the 1961 British comedy Don’t Bother to Knock, opposite Richard Todd, and was billed as one of the “six most exciting women in the world” alongside Melina Mercouri, Jeanne Moreau and Romy Schneider in Carl Foreman’s 1963 war fable, The Victors. Sommer’s Hollywood breakthrough arrived in the same year, with The Prize; she was cast as Paul Newman’s lover in an adaptation of Irving Wallace’s hit novel, for which she was a joint winner of a most promising newcomer Golden Globe.

Sommer’s Hollywood career then took off with A Shot in the Dark, in which she leaned heavily into her “sexpot” image as a maid suspected of a series of murders in the sequel to The Pink Panther, starring Peter Sellers. Following its success, Sommer appeared in a string of high profile Hollywood films, including The Art of Love with James Garner and Dick Van Dyke, The Oscar with Stephen Boyd, and the Bob Hope comedy Boy, Did I Get a Wrong Number! In 1968, she achieved leading actor status with The Wicked Dreams of Paula Schultz, a comedy about an East German athlete who pole-vaults over the Berlin Wall.

In the 1970s, Sommer appeared in two cult horror films by Mario Bava, Baron Blood and Lisa and the Devil, and sex comedies Percy and Percy’s Progress for British director Ralph Thomas. She followed these with two high-profile British films: as secretary Vera Clyde in And Then There Were None in 1974, adapted from Christie’s hit novel, and a year later, Carry on Behind, the 27th in the Carry On series.

After another Sellers film, The Prisoner of Zenda, and Ralph Thomas’s heist film A Nightingale Sang in Berkeley Square, Sommer scaled back her screen appearances and concentrated on painting. In the mid-1980s, she also became embroiled in a long-running feud with Zsa Zsa Gabor after they appeared together on TV show Circus of the Stars; Sommer was ultimately awarded $3.3m in damages for defamation.

Sommer was married twice, to writer Joe Hyams from 1964 until 1981, and hotelier Wolf Walther from 1993 until his death in 2026.

article_text:
Viele kennen Kandinskys Gemälde "Das bunte Leben" aus dem Münchner Lenbachhaus. 2023 wurde es als NS-Raubkunst eingestuft, nun wurde es in London versteigert - für viel Geld

Das berühmte Gemälde "Das bunte Leben" von Wassily Kandinsky, das Jahrzehnte im Münchner Lenbachhaus hing, ist für 27 Millionen Pfund (umgerechnet rund 32 Millionen Euro) versteigert worden. Das ergab die Auktion des Londoner Hauses Christie's am Abend. Das Gemälde war 2023 als NS-Raubkunst eingestuft und an die Erben der jüdischen Sammlerfamilie Lewenstein zurückgegeben worden.

Es handle sich "um ein wegweisendes Werk, das die Entwicklung der künstlerischen Formensprache des Künstlers auf den Punkt bringt und auf den außergewöhnlichen Wandel seines Stils in den darauffolgenden Jahren vorausweist", hatte Keith Gill von der Abteilung für Kunst des 20. und 21. Jahrhunderts bei Christie's zur Ankündigung der Aktion gesagt. Dabei sei es tief verbunden mit den kulturellen Traditionen von Kandinskys Heimat Russland.

Märchen mit altrussischen Motiven

"Das bunte Leben" mit altrussischen Motiven und märchenhaften Figuren wurde von Kandinsky (1866-1944) in seiner Pariser Zeit gemalt, unter dem Einfluss von Stilen wie dem Fauvismus, dem Symbolismus oder dem Jugendstil. 1907 wurde es laut Christie's zudem im Pariser Herbstsalon ausgestellt. Bis heute gilt es als Schlüsselwerk im Schaffen Kandinskys.

1927 erwarb es das Amsterdamer Sammlerehepaar Lewenstein. Nach dem Tod ihres Mannes Emanuel Albert Lewenstein (1870-1930) überließ seine Witwe Hedwig Lewenstein-Weyermann (1875-1937) das Temperabild dem Stedelijk Museum als Dauerleihgabe. Nach der Besetzung der Niederlande durch die Deutsche Wehrmacht wurde das Werk im Oktober 1940 versteigert - laut Christie's bekam der Sammler Salomon B. Slijper den Zuschlag. Dessen Familie verkaufte es 1972 der Bayerischen Landesbank (Bayern LB), die es 1973 als Dauerleihgabe ans Lenbachhaus übergab.

Jahrelanger Kampf um Rückgabe

Was folgte, war ein jahrelanger Kampf der Nachfahren der Lewensteins. Sie werteten die Auktion im Oktober 1940 als Unrecht und verlangten die Restitution. Ihre Argumentation: Die Familie habe das Bild 1938 bei einem Museum in Amsterdam zur Verwahrung gegeben, bevor sie vor den Nationalsozialisten in die USA floh. Ohne Erlaubnis sei es dann verkauft worden.

Die Provenienzforschung gab der Familie schließlich recht. Es fehle an Beweisen, dass sie das Gemälde 1940 aus freien Stücken beim Auktionshaus eingeliefert habe, befand die Beratende Kommission, die bis 2025 in Deutschland in strittigen Fragen der NS-Raubkunst Empfehlungen gab.

Den Recherchen der Kommission zufolge hatte ein Mitarbeiter des Museums das Bild im September 1940 «in unbekanntem Auftrag» mit Boten ins Auktionshaus bringen lassen und dort angeboten. Zahlreiche Indizien sprächen dafür, dass das Bild im Zusammenhang mit der systematischen Verfolgung der jüdischen Bevölkerung durch die Nazis entzogen worden sei, so die Kommission. Auch der Bayerische Landtag billigte 2023 die Rückgabe des Bildes.

article_text:
I n You Can See Everything , convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes invites film-makers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim into her home in a supposed act of “radical transparency”. Holmes is filmed, along with her partner, Billy Evans, and their two young children, in the weeks before starting a prison sentence for defrauding Theranos investors. “The best way for people to see who she is,” Evans says, “is to give as much access as possible into our daily lives”. It may also be the best way to market “Theranos 2.0”, which the couple are working on during filming. But the documentary questions whether Holmes is presenting her authentic self or a manufactured persona. Fielder speaks for the audience when he asks Holmes in a tense exchange whether she’s “being real” with him. “I’m always being real,” she says.

That question of authenticity is at the heart of documentary film-making. You Can See Everything is as much about the ambiguous relationship between film-maker and subject as it is about Holmes herself. There is often a power struggle over narrative control in documentaries, with both sides of the dynamic wanting different outcomes from the final film. Watching You Can See Everything inevitably prompts the question: why would Holmes, days before she heads to jail, invite the scrutiny of a film crew?

Some people, like Holmes, think a documentary will help rebuild their reputation after public disgrace. When Anthony Weiner, who resigned from Congress after tweeting a photo of his bulging groin, tried to stage a professional comeback with a New York mayoral bid, he allowed cameras to film the journey. Only, he had more to hide: when further sex scandals emerged, his campaign went from a story of public redemption to innuendo-laden humiliation. And all the while, the cameras kept rolling. Weiner is a prime example of a subject losing control of the narrative.

Weiner may have wanted a sympathetic portrayal, but he should have known that film-makers always have their own agendas. In the book The Journalist and the Murderer, Janet Malcolm reflects on the relationship between journalists and their subjects: “The subject becomes a kind of child of the writer, regarding him as a permissive, all-accepting, all-forgiving mother, and expecting the book to be written by her. Of course, the book is written by the strict, all-noticing, unforgiving father.” The same is surely true of the documentarian.

When Jackie and David Siegel allowed Lauren Greenfield to film their attempt to build a modern-day Versailles in Florida, the director wasn’t giving them free PR. Rather, with The Queen of Versailles , Greenfield was interested in the corrosive effects of extreme wealth. The Siegels agreed to be filmed because they were proud of their success. When their dream collapsed following the 2008 financial crash, The Queen of Versailles turned from a story of Xanadu-like grandeur to one of hubristic overreach. David later sued Lauren – unsuccessfully – for defamation, but he should have known from the beginning: it may have been his story, but it was never his film.

A few years after Versailles, Greenfield made The Kingmaker , about former first lady of the Philippines Imelda Marcos and her attempt to return the family to power. From the beginning of the film, Greenfield said , there was a power struggle over who was telling the story. Marcos, known for her lavish lifestyle during her husband’s brutal rule, understood the power of optics. In a children’s cancer ward, she hands out money to children in a public display of compassion. “Perception is real,” Marcos says in the film, “and the truth is not.”

Some people agree to projects believing they will have editorial control. Idi Amin gave Barbet Schroeder unprecedented access after the director essentially promised that they would make the film together. But Amin was unhappy with General Idi Amin Dada: A Self Portrait and demanded some footage be cut, rounding up more than 100 French residents in Uganda and holding them hostage until his demands were met. Schroeder agreed. It helps to be as ruthless as Amin if you want final cut.

Documentaries are often about the past, but some of cinema’s most memorable moments show people acting violently in the present, fully aware that they are being filmed. Frederick Wiseman’s austere films show abuse in psychiatric institutions (Titicut Follies) and horrific police violence (Law and Order). Why did people do unspeakable things in front of a camera? “People basically go about their business,” Wiseman told an interviewer , “and the presence of the camera doesn’t have much, if any effect on their behaviour.”

But cameras did have an effect on the subjects of Joshua Oppenheimer’s The Act of Killing , probably the most morally complex example of the film-maker-subject relationship in cinema history. Perpetrators of Indonesia’s mass killings gleefully re-enact their crimes, restaging their violent memories in the style of Hollywood movies. They do not profess their innocence. Rather, they agree to be filmed because they are proud of what they did. They really do want us to see everything.

Perhaps the most interesting case of someone willingly putting themselves under scrutiny is Lance Armstrong. Alex Gibney’s documentary on Armstrong was expected to be a puff piece. When the full extent of Armstrong’s doping was revealed, however, Gibney’s film changed direction, becoming a documentary not on a cyclist’s triumph but on a master manipulator who lied to everyone, including the film-maker. In The Armstrong Lie, Armstrong admits that he “was prepared to say anything” to keep his lie going.

Some people are simply arrogant enough to think they can get away with their lies. But others become so invested in their skewed version of reality that to refuse a documentary crew would be like admitting their deception. So they welcome the cameras, often doing more damage than if they had simply retreated from public view. But unlike Armstrong, Holmes still insists she has done nothing wrong. As she says in You Can See Everything: “I have nothing to hide.”

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Leslie Bibb is set to star in Upgraded 2 from director Becca Gleason, joining the previously announced returning star and producer Camila Mendes.

Luke Roberts and Justin Matthews, who penned the first film, wrote the screenplay. Story details are under wraps, but the first movie starred Mendes as Ana, an ambitious intern at an art auction house in New York City who misrepresents herself to a handsome wealthy man as the house’s director. As their romance develops, her deception creates challenges that threaten her career and relationship.

Related Stories

Leslie Bibb Went Off Book With Jean Smart In ‘Hacks’; Joins Brett Goldstein’s New ‘Escorted’ Show With Lesley Manville: “How Is This My Life?”

Leslie Bibb Stars In ‘The Rush Whisperer’ Sorority Recruitment Dark Comedy In Works At HBO

Gulfstream Pictures financed the original 2024 film. Amazon MGM Studios landed worldwide distribution rights to the sequel, which will be available in more than 240 countries and territories on Prime Video. It begins production this month in Italy.

Producers include Gulfstream’s Mike Karz and Bill Bindley, Honor Role’s Mendes and Rachel Matthews, Luber Roklin Entertainment’s Lena Roklin, and Tempo Productions’ Piers Tempest.

Watch on Deadline

Bibb most recently guest starred in Season 5 of HBO’s Hacks opposite Jean Smart and Hannah Einbinder, earning an Emmy nomination for Outstanding Guest Actress in a Comedy Series for the finale season. She also returned for the second season of Apple TV’s Emmy-nominated Palm Royale alongside Kristin Wiig, Allison Janney,and Laura Dern. Last year, Bibb starred in Season 3 of Mike White’s HBO drama The White Lotus and the ensemble earned an Actor Award nomination for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Drama Series.

Recently, it was announced that Bibb will star in and executive produce dark comedy series The Rush Whisperer for HBO . Also upcoming, she will star in Brett Goldstein’s romantic comedy series Escorted for Prime Video opposite Goldstein and Lesley Manville. Additional TV credits include Netflix’s original comedy God’s Favorite Idiot , Netflix’s superhero series Jupiter’s Legacy , ABC’s dramedy GCB , ABC’s American Housewife , TV Land’s Nobodies , NBC’s Crossing Jordan and the ninth season of NBC’s ER .

On the film side, her credits include Clint Eastwood’s Juror #2 ; Lionsgate’s About My Father ; The Lost Husband, which she also produced; Talladega Nights: The Ballad of Ricky Bobby ; Iron Man and Iron Man 2; Warner Bros’ comedy Tag; Netflix’s To the Bone; Jared Hess’ Don Verdeen; No Good Deed ; Hell Baby; Sony’s Zookeeper; Take Care; Confessions of a Shopaholic; Law Abiding Citizen; A Good Old Fashioned Orgy ; and Miss Nobody.

Bibb is represented by UTA, LBI and JSSK.

article_text:
It’s late January, and the intrepid Film Comment crew is on the ground reporting from an extra special edition of the Sundance Film Festival—the last to take place on the snowy slopes of Park City, Utah, the festival’s home since 1981, before moving to Boulder, Colorado in 2027. For the next week, we’ll be gathering the best critics on the scene to talk about each day’s premieres on the Podcast.

To kick things off, Film Comment Editor Devika Girish invited programmer Madeline Whittle (Film at Lincoln Center) as well as critics Robert Daniels (RogerEbert.com) and Will Tavlin ( n+1 ) to share their responses to the films premiering during the first few days of the fest. The group discusses the tongue-in-cheek Charli XCX mockumentary The Moment (3:30), Casper Kelly’s dark comedy Buddy (20:15), and Beth de Araujo’s sophomore feature Josephine (29:50).

title_original: How Cringe Took Over Culture
editorial_title_zh: 尴尬如何接管了文化
editorial_excerpt_zh: 当你看到尴尬时，你就能认出它。但它究竟是什么？
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "在艺术中，正如在生活中一样，肉体凌乱的物质性丝毫不会让我退缩。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "鲁卡斯·穆迪森（Lukas Moodysson）的《心海怒涛》（2004）的高潮部分，吉科（Geko）吐在了苔丝（Tess）张开的嘴里？我写过它。朱迪·芝加哥（Judy Chicago）对经血的公然抗拒、伊娜·波普（Ina Poppe）的母乳奶酪、马丁·冯·奥斯特罗夫斯基（Martin von Ostrowski）涂满精液的画布、马克·奎因（Marc Quinn）用10品脱自己的血浇筑的雕塑？这全在我的好球区。今年奥地利馆里弗洛伦蒂娜·霍尔辛格（Florentina Holzinger）处理排泄物、在尿液中打滚的威尼斯海洋世界？我爱极了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，在观看克里斯托弗·博格利（Kristoffer Borgli）的电影《The Drama》（2026）的院线放映20分钟后，我发现自己陷入了一种绝对痛苦的姿势：双膝抱胸、双肩驼起，衬衫领子拉到眼睛下方，随时准备将脸完全遮住，紧张感让我的下巴扭曲。这是一个身体试图将自己缩小并消失在一个单点中的徒劳尝试。所有这些痛苦的直接原因是什么？是一场朋友间的谈话。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "孩子们对这里发生的事情有一个词。哲学家们也是。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尴尬（Cringe）。这是一个描述旧事物的全新术语。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "它连接了两种情感：羞耻与同情。羞耻的历史更悠久——无论是夏娃还是马萨乔对此都不陌生。源自意为“遮蔽”的词根，它将内疚、耻辱和不光彩融为一体，并与惩戒（想想安德烈娅·比特纳[Andrea Büttner]2022–25年关于公开羞辱的丝网版画）、赤裸的脆弱（在珍妮·萨维尔[Jenny Saville]1993年的作品《计划》的极端的角度中形式化）以及揭露本应隐藏之物的行为（正如特雷西·艾敏[Tracey Emin]1995年的《我曾与他睡过的所有人 1963–1995》或马丁·西姆斯[Martine Syms]2020年的日记式摄影集《羞耻空间》[Shame Space]中所展现的那样）紧密相连。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/avpc_r2_rec709_g24_3996x2160_0178583.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "赞达亚与罗伯特·帕丁森出演的《The Drama》。图片由 A24 提供", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在这种痛苦的体验中，一个人暴露无遗（即脸红背叛了自己），并渴望将自己藏起来。或者彻底抹杀自我——因羞耻而死并不总是一个比喻。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "同情来得更晚，它在18世纪的思想中通过亚当·斯密的《道德情操论》（1759）被释放出来。斯密将《马太福音》7:12中的基督教律法（“你们愿意人怎样待你们，你们也要怎样待人”云云）世俗化和理性化，他坚信“公正的旁观者”的想象力可以通过表现如果我们“处于”他们的处境“会”作何感觉，来构想他人情感体验的概念：“我们设想自己忍受着所有同样的折磨，我们仿佛进入了他的身体，在某种程度上与他成为了同一个人。”而且这不仅仅是我们能够与他人感同身受，更是我们应该这样做：斯密写下的正是一部伦理学著作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尴尬就是同情的羞耻。移情性的尴尬。代理性的丢脸。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "每种语言都有一个词来形容这种令人不快的体验。在荷兰语中，plaatsvervangende schaamte 是替代性羞耻。法语的 gêne par procuration 将不适感转嫁他人，而德语的 Fremdschämen 意味着异己的羞耻。瑞典语中有 skämskudde，即“尴尬抱枕”，在观看例如全球电视直播的霹雳舞失误时，人们会把脸埋进这个枕头里。在日语中，mite irarenai 意为无法直视某事（令人痛苦、尴尬、灾难性），但中文网络俚语“尴尬癌”（gāngà’ái）才是真正的赢家。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如今，这个感叹词在网络上发挥了很大作用，成了一种全方位的贬义代名词。对尴尬进行治安管理是互联网最残酷的职业——它是骚扰活动和蔑视平台化的根源。数字弱势群体的四大骑士——酷儿、神经多样性群体、经济不安定者和社交孤立者——其热情、努力和普遍存在的最容易被宣布为令人反感或可悲。", article_text:
In art, as in life, the messy materiality of flesh fazes me not one whit.

The climax of Lukas Moodysson’s A Hole in My Heart (2004), where Geko vomits into Tess’s open mouth? Wrote about it. Judy Chicago’s menstrual defiance , Ina Poppe’s mother’s milk cheese, Martin von Ostrowski’s spunk-strewn canvases, Marc Quinn’s sculpture cast with 10 pints of his own blood? Up my alley. Florentina Holzinger’s waste-processing, piss-wallowing Seaworld Venice at this year’s Austrian Pavilion? Love it.

Yet 20 minutes into a theatrical screening of Kristoffer Borgli’s The Drama (2026), I found myself in a posture of absolute misery: knees drawn to chest, shoulders hunched, the collar of my shirt pulled up under my eyes ready to cover them entirely, tension contorting my jaw. A body’s futile attempt to disappear into a single point. The proximate cause of all this anguish? A conversation among friends.

The kids have a word for what happened here. So do the philosophers.

Cringe. It’s a new term for an old thing.

It bridges two affects: shame and sympathy. Shame is older—news to neither Eve nor Masaccio. From the root “to cover,” its mix of guilt, disgrace, and dishonor is bonded to castigation (think Andrea Büttner’s 2022–25 serigraphs of public humiliation), the vulnerability of nakedness (formalized in the extreme angle of Jenny Saville’s 1993 Plan ), and the revelation of what ought to remain hidden (as in Tracey Emin’s 1995 Everyone I Have Ever Slept With 1963–1995 or Martine Syms’s diaristic 2020 photobook, Shame Space ).

In this painful experience, one is exposed (the betrayal that is blushing) and longs to hide oneself. Or obliterate the self—dying of shame is not always a metaphor.

Sympathy comes later, unleashed in 18th-century thought through Adam Smith’s Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759). Secularizing and rationalizing the Christian law of Matthew 7:12 (“Do unto others” and all that), Smith insists that the imagination of an “impartial spectator” can form a conception of the emotional experience of another by representing how we would feel “if we were” in their situation: “We conceive ourselves enduring all the same torments, we enter, as it were, into his body, and become in some measure the same person with him.” And it is not merely that we can feel with others, but that we should: Smith is writing an ethics.

Cringe is sympathetic shame. Vicarious embarrassment. Mortification by proxy.

EVERY LANGUAGE HAS has a name for this unpleasant experience. In Dutch, plaatsvervangende schaamte is substitute shame. The French gêne par procuration delegates discomfort, while the German Fremdschämen means foreign shame.Swedish has the skämskudde , a “cringe cushion” in which to bury one’s face while watching, say, a globally televised breakdancing fail. In Japanese, mite irarenai means unable to look at something (distressing, awkward, disastrous), but it’s Chinese slang for the win with gāngà’ái : embarrassment cancer.

These days, the interjection does a lot of work online as an all-purpose signifier of derogation. Policing cringe is the cruelest métier of the internet—the origin of harassment campaigns and platforming of contempt. The Four Horsemen of the digitally vulnerable—the queer, neurodivergent, economically precarious, and socially isolated—are far more likely to have their enthusiasms, efforts, and general being declared repellent or pathetic.

Upon receiving an honorary degree in 2022, Taylor Swift urged graduates to “learn to live alongside cringe.” But we all know that while a pretty white girl’s earnestness may read as adorkable authenticity, that advice is tone-deaf at best, insensitive at worst to so many.

Even in its less-noxious forms, to declare something “so cringe” is inherently censorious. “ Hamilton is cringe!”flings Gen Alpha at their elders’ damp-eyed civic credulity; “Your nonsensical skibidi toilet rizz is cringe,” the millennials reply. Such generational accusations get tiresome quickly. Everyone thinks their kids’ slang is ridiculous and their parents’ politics naive.

BUT BEHIND THE epithet’s online omnipresence is a serious aesthetic affect grouped among strong sensations that act on the body—terms like disgust (dis-taste: what one wants to spit out) or horror (from the Latin horrere : bristling hair). Its flinching recoil derives from the Old English cringan : to yield or fall (as in battle), eventually suggesting crouching in fear.

While disgust claims the stomach and horror the nape, cringe assails the muscles of the face: a spectacle half-watched through half-narrowed eyes above a half-opened rictus.

Cringe’s temporality is complex. Wincing—its signature gesture—is sharp, sudden, violent. But duration turns the screw—prolonged humiliation or a slow unfolding toward future self-recrimination.

Is the cringeworthy utterly individual? Yes and no.

It is like obscenity, in that you know it when you see it—except when you don’t and find yourself repelled or turned on by something self-evidently arousing or repulsive to someone else, and feel yourself exposed in having failed to have known it when you saw it.

Cringing can therefore manifest as the abashment of not knowing (yet; possibly ever) how to read something. Most harrowing in Torbjørn Rødland’s This Is My Body (2013–15)—a luminous photograph of a girl’s head tilted upward by adult male hands whose fingers caress the edge of her mouth—is the realization that we cannot know whether we are witnessing bliss or brutality.

In Diego Marcon ’s video The Parents’ Room (2021), a prosthetically masked man sings of the murders of his wife and children, then of his suicide. The video plays hopscotch with tone—at once horrific, ridiculous, and bathetically earnest. To mock or to mourn? That is the (distressing) question.

Or consider Jordan Strafer’s trilogy— Loophole (2023), Decadence (2024), and Talk Show (2026)—the last of which was shown in this year’s Whitney Biennial. It traffics in the somber content of trauma and sexual assault, yet performances are stylized beyond even the clichés of melodrama. Guiltily, we wonder: Are these testimonial figures worthy of compassion or not?

Complicating matters, one person’s cringe is another’s enjoyment. If X thinks some event will never befall them, or if they disallow any similarity to Y, then X might relish the spectacle of Y’s mortification—this is schadenfreude. If, however, I feel sympathy with Y on any grounds, then their humiliation is mine as well.

The playwright Aristophanes’ account of love was the soul’s clocking of its like in another. As goes eros, so goes shame. To cringe is to recognize.

Cringe thereby exposes a political truth: With whom do we feel we share something in common? It is an aesthetic reaction that strips bare one’s ethics of identification.

NOT ALL ART THAT discomfits is cringe. Damien Hirst’s A Thousand Years (1990) confronts viewers with its vitrine containing a severed cow’s head and maggots-cum-flies. It may turn stomachs, but it lacks the minefield of social relationality.

Although one can be ashamed of one’s former self (give the teenage poet a decade), cringe is inherently interpersonal, bound up with anxieties around social rejection. It scripts the interrogatory diagram where the collective meets the psychic: How do others regard me? As a joke? As talented? As a freak, a threat, an object of desire? A “chilled-out entertainer” of a boss? Da Ya Think I’m Sexy? Do you think I’m cool?

The Drama staged this structure in the process of fracturing. Dining with her fiancé and close friends, a woman imagines she is speaking within a shared set of social norms as they each playfully admit the “worst thing” they’ve ever done. But at her turn, it becomes clear that she has revealed the wrong sort of vulnerability. In place of the intimacy that the other revelations engender, hers marks her as different. What ensues is the complete batshit breakdown of every form of relationality in the film.

Nor is that all. The pain of cringe compounds. In my disturbance—whether witnessed by a fellow cinema patron or a reader of this essay—I am exposed a second time. In unconcealing what you find cringeworthy, cringe is secondhand shame that yields a firsthand confession.

For my body has betrayed that my personal Room 101 must be the mid-exposure realization of having miscalculated a mutual understanding.

LODGED IN THIS GAP between one’s self – image and someone else’s perception, all cringe art is, on some level, performance art.

The School of Athens for first-generation cringe therefore includes 1970s body art (Abramović and Acconci, our deputized Plato and Aristotle), the anti-comedy of Andy Kaufman, and Viennese Actionism. Its iteration in the 1980s and 1990s includes some YBAs (Sarah Lucas) and the sick aesthetics of Paul McCarthy and Mike Kelley—witness the glorious banner reading pants shitter & proud p.s. jerk-off too (and i wear glasses) of Kelley’s 1987 Three Point Program/Four Eyes . Ryan Trecartin is the manic heir apparent to this trash-culture bloodline, updating it for a hyperperformative age.

In the term’s modern era, media scholars point to an influential run of “cringe comedy” in quality television in the 2000s. The aughts had the fraternity of Curb Your Enthusiasm , Da Ali G Show , The Office (UK), and Peep Show . A decade later saw the feminist rejoinder: The Comeback , Girls , Veep , Crazy Ex-Girlfriend , Insecure , and Fleabag .

In this golden age of cringe, that earlier art of transgression—with its tense silences, humiliations, and hostile disturbance of the performer-audience relationship—was channeled downstream. One could program the Girls Q-tip scene alongside Abramović’s Rhythm 0 . And although they might not have the cultural capital of Acconci’s now-canonical Seedbed —in which he masturbated under a ramp while detailing his fantasies of the visitors walking above him—shows like Nathan for You and The Rehearsal have allowed Nathan Fielder to make a career off the same unwilled voyeurism experienced by those gallery visitors of 1972.

THE EXPRESSIVE POSSIBILITIES of cringe have been subsequently taken up by a range of artists working today. But first, an important distinction.

There is what I’ll call minor cringe —art that is about cringe but consumable with nary a wince. Minor cringe is meta-cringe , standing apart from the affect while coolly investigating it.

Major cringe , on the other hand, navigates the aesthetic affect critically and formally to induce it—viscerally exploiting its possibilities. Major cringe is endo-cringe . It is within it; totally saturated by it.

A Geschämtkunstwerk , if you will.

The distinction is piece by piece; the same artist can produce both. Christine Tien Wang’s photorealistic meme paintings in her 2022 exhibition “Fake Stupid, queen of cringe” at Galerie Nagel Draxler in Berlin were minor cringe. Taking a bird’s-eye view of the affects of network culture—shame, snark, anxiety—they were, nevertheless, affectively innocuous.

Not so with Starving Artist (2025), a canvas depicting a computer screen with multiple windows: a spreadsheet of bitcoin investments; the spine of a James Joyce novel; a meme based on the film Challengers ; and an archival photograph of a victim of famine. Wang’s acrylic (re)rendering forces a reckoning with the moral stakes of algorithmic flattening. Shame is platformed. A portrait of collective responsibility for elisions between historical trauma and its ironized circulation? Major cringe.

Nor does an artist progress from one to the other; they are merely different modes. Amalia Ulman’s 2025 film Magic Farm , about an American team’s desperation to manufacture a viral trend in rural Argentina, is minor cringe for its pleasurable skewering of the attention economy. Her Instagram long-form project Excellences & Perfections , from 2014, however, was major cringe. Why? Because its documentation of an extreme makeover in the vernacular of online self-modification involved aspects that were fabricated (her staged breast augmentation) and nonfabricated (her actual extreme food restriction). Vicarious disturbance bleeds into complicity in an era when self-representation is conflated with self-branding. There is no position outside of cringe here.

ANY HUMILIATION IS a fall—the term descends from humilis , “on the ground.” Accordingly, many modern-day interlocutors of cringe are infatuated with the grotesque performative contortions required by life as a woman. Elevated ideals can only crumble.

Several of those dragomans were included in the recent exhibition “Picture Perfect” at Bozar in Brussels, which ran from March to August of this year. The show sought to expand norms of representation—a project whose sincerity all but courts the cringeworthy—with artists hell-bent on deconstructing the drive for beauty, including Orlan, Sara Cwynar, Juno Calypso, and Haley Morris-Cafiero. Their works render femininity disgustingly cute, violently expressed, and contemptuously received by others—both when it fails and when it succeeds. Ideals are nightmares that way.

Marianna Simnett’s video Blue Moon (2022) was on display: a glitching, flute-playing, Athena-like figure continuously morphing into a teal-and-tawny palette. Athena is herself an allegory about cringe—as the story goes, she abandoned and cursed her beloved flute after seeing how her cheeks puffed out while playing. That a self-image forged in the crucible of the fear of being ugly makes women amputate their talents? Sixteenth century BCE, meet 2026.

Or regard Anna Uddenberg’s sculpture Focus #2 (Pussy Padding) , 2018, on display at the Boros Collection in Berlin from 2022 to 2026. It assembles acrylic nails, resin and fiberglass, vinyl film, and a barstool to construct a female body bent in half as she extends a fake-fur–covered selfie stick over plastic-vented genitalia. The work is tacky in signifiers, excruciating in implication. The materials are the point: The more strictly synthetics are enlisted to illustrate a ludicrous eroticism, the more embarrassed we are to recognize the deforming desire to be desired.

The apotheosis of this aesthetic of thirstiness is found in the paintings of Catherine Mulligan. Her solo show “Bad Girls Club” at Tara Downs in 2023 featured grotesque women seductively posed, decked out in the mien of late-millennial glam-trash McBling. The hands are a masterclass in contrast: Elongated nails resemble girlie self-care and melting flesh. Pouting lips are blow-job ready and corpse-bloated, flesh so bronzed it’s purple-gray. These half-dead bodies are so desperate for the world’s approval that their forms distort the pictorial, skewing perspective and leaching collaged text onto the sides of the frames.

Despite its bond with performance, cringe finds its medial match in such figurative painting. No accident that the likes of Lisa Yuskavage, Sasha Gordon, and Mulligan are regularly invoked in accounts of cringe-adjacent concepts like abjection, disturbance, disquiet. These painter’s painters retain a bond to recognizable forms of the real. To the extent that cringe feeds off sympathy and recognition, it blossoms where tropes, figures, and types play.

One can thus imagine a shocking or rage-inducing abstract painting—the history of iconoclasm attests to this. But it is impossible to imagine a purely abstract painting in relation to cringe except as a bland metaphor for dislike. Cringe qua cringe is tethered to the social. It is most acute where it is most iconic.

BEING THAT NETWORK culture is a constant inducement to exhibitionism, the internet is an incubator for public humiliation suo nomine . Accordingly, it has exponentially expanded the possibilities for humiliation by proxy.

Made early in this era, Elisa Giardina Papa’s need ideas!?! PLZ!! (2011) is a compilation of YouTube clips of young teenagers attempting to generate viewership for their vlogs. Addressing the camera, guileless eyes above baby-fat cheeks entreat: “Hey uhm YouTube, it’s PinkSummerCrush, uhm… I wanted to start a web show and I need ideas for it but I don’t know, like, any ideas.” Another whispers, “I don’t know what to do so give me ideas. I’m trying to get more stuff done. Please send me ideas… please.”

These implorations are issued from childish bedrooms with an innocence oblivious to innuendo: “I want to make you guys happy” pleads one; “I’ll do anything except for sticking something up my nose” says another. Some both beg for ideas and announce they have zero subscribers, importing the possibility that no one is watching at all.

No flayed martyr has anything on a teenage girl. Her exposure is total—her vulnerability pleromatic.

This is major cringe at its limit. Not merely due to sympathy for the tweens, nor from projecting some future time when the unerasable archive of this yearning might prove embarrassing.

Rather, to live under platform capitalism is to recognize the disturbing manner in which human need has been redescribed as algorithmic entanglement. Pretend you haven’t heard these phrases before and bear their weight: Please like this . I’ll do anything . Follow me .

Cringe names our ethical recognition of the stakes of emptying out these words.

FINALLY, THE TOUCHIEST question—the one that touches on taste. What about art that makes one cringe with embarrassment at its existence? For some, it’s the intentional kitsch of Neo-Pop; for others, the whole Jay-Z/Marina Abramović thing. I’ll nominate luxury-brand collaborations—the artworld’s driest thirst trap.

But can we learn something from art that makes us feel this way? Something, perhaps, about time? Historical time, that is.

Recall Nikki S. Lee’s “Projects,” made between 1997 and 2001, in which she photographed herself passing among various social groups and subcultures. Perhaps you, like I, were around for its heyday.

It is said that today’s poor taste is tomorrow’s high art. Cringe works in reverse: What was high art yesterday can seem like a lapse in taste today.

For who can look now at the darkened face and box braids of the Korean American photographer in her “Hip Hop Project” without wincing? (Cue a second grimace for that title.) Conversations around racial caricature have evolved; what was edgy feels painfully passé.

Yet we can learn from cringe, so long as we stay closer to Smith’s moral sentiments than online callout culture. For cringe instructs us in the humility of taste—of our aesthetic fashions, of how we ask aesthetics to do politics in certain moments. Cringing at a dated work of art is a reminder of the fragility of all of our judgments.

It has become fashionable lately to condemn sympathy for appropriating the misery of others. I remain convinced, however, that there is no truly good alternative. The sympathetic shame of cringe is the price of sociality. We live among others and have the extraordinary capacity to sometimes suffer as they do.

Who would want the callous world that successfully cloistered the feelings of others? Cringe may be excruciating, but post-cringe would be pure horror.

"作品的尺寸各不相同，有些摄影作品出奇地大，不过人们并不总能明白，为什么某一特定主题要从紧凑的私密感中被剥离放大出来。比如那些真人大小的漫画形象，它们从梦工厂误打误撞地来到了曼哈顿正中央的现实中。在短暂的一笑之后，它们便死于一个过于陈腐的笑梗。艾丁格对此甘之如饴，因为他知道如何在其他途径中从生活中汲取出令人卸下防备的忧郁时刻。", "translated": true}, {"type": article_text:
Auf der Leinwand führt gerade kein Weg an Lars Eidinger vorbei. Doch auch als Fotograf ist er Stammgast in deutschen Museen. In der Kunsthalle Tübingen nimmt er es mit der Sammlung auf - und zeigt sein Gespür für die kleinen Dinge am Rande

An Einkaufswagen als Sinnbild der Konsumgesellschaft herrscht in der jüngsten Kunstgeschichte eigentlich kein Mangel: angefangen beim "Supermarket Shopper" von Douane Hanson bis zu Alexandra Birckens in zwei Hälften aufgeschnittener Skulptur "Descartes". Der Schauspieler Lars Eidinger , der zuletzt seine Smartphone-Fotos in großen Museen von Hamburg bis Düsseldorf ausstellte, meinte wohl, seinen Radius erweitern zu müssen. Denn warum sonst hat er sich trotz der längst auserzählten Motivkette ein auf der Straße pittoresk verrostetes Exemplar in seine neue Ausstellung "Present Perfect" in Tübingen gestellt?

Auf die Frage, ob es sich bei dem Einkaufswagen-Readymade um einen Kommentar auf die vielen Krisen des Postkapitalismus handelt, sagt Eidinger im Gespräch nur, dass es ihm nicht um Gesellschaftskritik gehe. Die Interpretation überlasse er den Betrachtern.

Also fällt man beim Gang durch die Ausstellung ganz automatisch in die individuelle Analyse. Und steht zum Beispiel gleich am Anfang, wo Eidingers Karriere als Schauspieler entlang von Fotos und Filmausschnitten aufgefächert wird, vor seinem kindlichen Selbstporträt als Hamster von 1982. Das bemitleidenswerte Tier steckt in einem unscharf aufgenommenen Wohnraum in einer Klopapierrolle fest.

Fotografie als Ausweg aus der Enge

Da sprudelt die Interpretation dann doch aus Eidinger heraus, und er berichtet von der einengenden Atmosphäre, in der er aufgewachsen sei. Zum Fotografieren als Ausweg gesellte sich in der Pubertät das Aufnehmen von Schallplatten. An einem Beweisstück für seine bis heute andauernde Aktivität als DJ kommt man ebensowenig vorbei wie an seinem grandiosen Porträt von Juergen Teller, das Eidinger in seiner legendären Theaterrolle als Hamlet zeigt.

Derart gründlich eingestimmt taucht man erwartungsvoll in den angenehm luftig gestalteten Parcours aus Fotos und Videos ein. Die Mehrheit ist im Stil klassischer Street- und Alltagsfotografie gehalten und wird erstmals im Dialog mit Werken aus der Sammlung der Kunsthalle Tübingen gezeigt.

Direktorin Nicole Fritz hatte mit dem dauerreisenden Eidinger im Vorfeld per WhatsApp kommuniziert und die Ausstellung am Computer virtuell vorinszeniert. Erst bei der Hängung wirkte der Künstler leibhaftig mit. In die endgültige Auswahl der von ihr vorgeschlagenen Positionen schafften es Werke von Yves Klein, Claes Oldenburg, Carl Andre, Erwin Wurm oder Katja Strunz. Dazwischen, stets doppelbödig und mit Sinn für verblüffende Referenzen abgestimmt, gibt es Eidingers frühere, teils schon mehrfach ausgestellte Arbeiten zu sehen. Aber seine neuen und ganz frischen Bilder dominieren.

Entwaffnend melancholische Momente

Die Formate sind unterschiedlich, manche Aufnahmen sind ausgesprochen groß, wobei nicht immer klar wird, warum das jeweilige Motiv aus der Intimität des Kompakten herausgehoben wird. Wie etwa die lebensgroßen Comic-Figuren, die sich mitten in Manhattan aus der Traumfabrik in die Realität verirrt haben. Nach einem kurzen Schmunzeln sterben sie den Tod eines allzu banalen Gags. Das nimmt Eidinger in Kauf, weiß er doch auf anderen Pfaden dem Leben entwaffnend melancholische Momente abzugewinnen.

Außerdem weiß er, an wem er sich orientiert: an Fotografen wie Juergen Teller oder William Eggleston, mit denen ihn Bilder verbinden, die wie beiläufig "aus der Hüfte geschossen" wirken.

Seltsamerweise fehlt Martin Parr in seiner Inspirations-Liste, mit dem er den satirischen Blick auf den Alltag teilt. Der kürzlich verstorbene Brite hielt die Absurditäten der Konsumkultur in grellen, kontrastreichen Farben fest. Eidinger gibt sich da zurückhaltender, ist aber ähnlich empfänglich für widersprüchliche bis erschütternde Momente im urbanen Raum.

Das Spiel der Wechselwirkungen

Es sind die kleinen Dinge am Rande, die seine Aufmerksamkeit instinktiv erregen: ein Wachmann, der im Pariser Grand Palais einen Blick in die Schnee-Kulissen einer Modenschau von Karl Lagerfeld wagt, eine verfaulte Banane als memento mori in einem Fahrradkorb, die vielen sich selbst überlassenen Obdachlosen oder - aus der Corona-Zeit - maskierte Besuchermassen vor dem Gemälde "Die Hochzeit zu Kana" von Paolo Veronese im Louvre, auf dem sich eine ähnlich ausufernde Figurenkonzentration spiegelt.

Geradezu seismographisch gerät das Porträt einer jungen Japanerin. Aufwändig gestylt posiert sie auf einer verspiegelten Bühne für ein Selfie. Das zwanghafte Starren auf gleich zwei Smartphones hindert sie daran, den magischen Moment ihrer Spiegelung inmitten eines wild blühenden Gartens wahrzunehmen. Auf diese narzisstische Isolation reagiert gegenüber Ben Willikens' Gemälde "Raum A1" von 1978, das ein menschenleeres, in kühles Grau getauchtes Zimmer zeigt.

Das Spiel der dialogischen Wechselwirkungen setzt sich mit Sigmar Polkes "Die Fahrt auf der Unendlichkeitsacht I" von 1969–71 fort, einem monumentalen Gemälde, auf dem es von gekritzelten Zeichen und Bildfragmenten wimmelt; ähnlich denen, die Eidinger bei seinen Exkursionen im Stadtraum entdeckt. Oder mit Daniel Spoerris "Variation d’un petit déjeuner" von 1967, einem Stillleben von Gläsern und Bestecken, die nach dem Frühstück auf einem Tisch übrig geblieben sind und die auf Eidingers unerschöpfliche Sammlung visueller Fundstücke verweisen.

Zu guter Letzt sind da noch die vielen diskreten Aufnahmen von sich unbeobachtet wähnenden Passanten, meistens von hinten oder im Profil aufgenommen. In einer eng gehängten Serie gleichen sie sich in Kleidung und Körperhaltung, darunter Freundinnen, Paare, Hundebesitzer und anarchische Kinder, die sich an Geldautomaten vergreifen.

Ode an den besessen knipsenden Großstadt-Flaneur

Sie alle mutieren zu unfreiwilligen Wiedergängern. Der Ansatz weist wie ein Echo auf Martin Parrs Projekt "Déjà View" zurück. Ausgehend von seinen ikonischen Farbfotografien, konfrontierte er diese mit historischen Amateur-Farbdias aus den 1950er- bis 1980er-Jahren. Und siehe da, die "Doppelgänger"-Bilder von Strandurlaubern überraschten mit identischen Posen, denselben Kombinationen aus Socken und Sandalen oder exakt gleichen Mustern der Kleidung.

Bei so vielen Analogien unter wahrverwandten Foto-Anthropologen wechselt man lieber das Medium und taucht in Eidingers Videos ein, etwa in die beinahe abstrakt wirkenden Muster von ineinander verknoteten Rolltreppen, oder in Wohnräume, in denen unscheinbare Objekte im Windzug ein Eigenleben entwickeln. Nicht zu vergessen Erwin Wurms Skulptur "Lars Departing", für die Eidinger drei Stunden auf einem Bein mit erhobenem Arm posierte.

Eigentlich ein sinnloses Unterfangen, denn Wurm ließ es sich nicht nehmen, den abgeformten Körper nach seinem Gusto zu deformieren - immerhin für die museale Ewigkeit. Und eben jener ist Eidinger mit dieser stimmigen Ode an den besessen knipsenden Großstadt-Flaneur einen weiteren Schritt näher gekommen.

He speaks to Isaac Huxtable"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Misan Harriman has a captive audience. Five years ago the London-based portrait photographer was an extremely established practitioner, top of his game, magazine covers across the newsstands, the man selected for Meghan and Harry Sussex’s baby announcement (and baby reveal). A proud and politically active Black man, Harriman was a shining exemplar in shifting editorial times. Black Lives Matter had shaken the fashion/editorial/publication worlds, and essential, overdue attention was being given to Black artists, celebrities, thinkers, politicians. Often they were photographed by Harriman. He has worked with Steve McQueen, Lewis Hamilton, Diane Abbott, Naomi Campbell and Marcus Rashford, to name but a few. He is also the first Black photographer in the century-long history of British Vogue to shoot the September issue cover. In July 2021, he became chair of the Southbank Centre, London."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Harriman built a platform and audience throughout his rise, attracting people who appreciate the twin flames of artistic production and political activism. He is a star photographer. But his Blackness, his politics, his belief in human value, and the actual point of all this representation is rooted in Black political thought. Sometimes the sumptuous photograph and the vocal photographer do not mix with ease, as was the case for Gordon Parks, one of his inspirations. Harriman is a man of principles, and principles have a cost. He knows why he makes these photographs, and he refuses to be silenced. A week after this interview, amid calls for Harriman to be removed from his position as chair of the Southbank Centre due to social media posts, the photographer announced he will not seek another term.
